report.currency: USD (tables in $ millions unless stated; market reports natively in USD — no FX conversion required)
report.verdict: Maryland is a mature, almost entirely mobile (98%+) sports-betting market that is still compounding volume — 9M 2026 handle $4,983.7m, +9% YoY, Q3 +11.4% — but gross win has decoupled from stakes: Q3 GGR fell 6.4% to $159.2m on a 9.9% hold and September GGR fell 20% at a 9.0% hold, so state receipts dropped 17.5% in Q3 despite the 20% mobile rate introduced in July 2025. The regulatory direction is toward higher fiscal extraction and perimeter defence (prediction markets, unlicensed online gaming) rather than product expansion, with iGaming still unlegalised and six land-based casinos flat-to-down (Q3 GGR $469.3m, −4%).

summary: **Handle nearing $5bn but decelerating:** Maryland sportsbooks took $4,983.7m in stakes in Jan–Sep 2026 (sum of MLGCA monthly releases), +9% YoY per Gaming Intelligence (9M 2025 implied ≈$4.57bn). Q3 handle of $1,614.5m was +11.4% vs the regulator's FY2026 Q1 figure of $1,449.3m, but September was flat (+0.2% to $652.2m vs $651.0m) — the weakest YoY print of the year.

**GGR has decoupled from volume:** 9M gross win (handle less prizes) was $533.2m at a 10.7% hold. H1 hold was 11.1% but Q3 slipped to 9.9% (vs 11.7% in Q3 2025), taking Q3 GGR down 6.4% to $159.2m; September GGR was $58.5m, −20.0% YoY, at 9.0% (mobile 8.8%).

**State take falling despite a higher rate:** 9M 2026 contributions were $78.3m (Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund $59.0m; General Fund $19.3m). Q3 was $24.6m, −17.5% vs $29.8m, and September $9.1m, −32.5% vs $13.5m. Both comparison periods were already at the 20% mobile rate, so the decline is entirely hold/promo-driven, not rate-driven.

**Mobile is the market:** mobile accounted for 98.4% of Q3 handle ($1,589.1m vs $25.4m retail) and 98.3% in September ($641.2m vs $11.0m). Retail is a brand touchpoint: Q3 retail GGR $3.0m, retail tax $0.41m.

**Tax regime — GGR-based with deductions:** the base is 'taxable win' = hold less deductible free promotional wagers and 'other amounts' (reconciles to the 0.25% federal excise on handle). Retail pays 15% to the Blueprint Fund; mobile pays 20% (15% Blueprint + 5% General Fund) since 1 July 2025, up from 15%. Taxable win was 73.7% of GGR in 9M ($393.1m), giving an effective 14.7% of GGR.

**Promo intensity is modest and falling:** deductible mobile promotional wagers were $31.6m in Q3 (2.0% of mobile handle: Jul 2.4%, Aug 1.9%, Sep 1.7%). Total deductions in 9M were $140.1m (26.3% of GGR), of which an estimated $12.5m is federal excise.

**FY2026 was a record year for the Treasury:** sports wagering returned $132.3m in FY2026 (Jul 2025–Jun 2026), +49% vs $88.9m in FY2025, helped by the five-point rate rise; the Lottery, casinos and sports wagering together contributed a record $1.637bn to the state in FY2026 (Maryland Lottery release, 7 Aug 2026).

**FY2027 has started lower:** Q1 FY2027 (Jul–Sep 2026) contributions of $24.6m compare with $29.8m a year earlier; July was +16.6% ($8.45m vs $7.25m) but August ($7.0m) and September ($9.1m) fell sharply on low hold.

**Cumulative programme yield:** since launch in Dec 2021 sports wagering has paid $295.6m to the Blueprint Fund, $38.6m to the General Fund and $5.8m of expired prizes (unclaimed after 182 days) to the Problem Gambling Fund — ≈$340m in total, excluding licence fees.

**Casinos are flat-to-down:** the six casinos generated $151.4m in September (−0.1% YoY), $160.0m in August and $157.9m in July — Q3 GGR $469.3m, −4% YoY per Gaming Intelligence — an annualised ~$1.9bn land-based market with no growth engine while iGaming remains illegal.

**Operator landscape — nine mobile brands, duopoly-led:** the September data cover bet365, BetMGM, betPARX, BetRivers, Caesars, DraftKings, Fanatics, FanDuel and theScore Bet (per the lead coverage's tags). FanDuel and DraftKings lead; operator-level shares are n/a here (the regulator's operator Excel was not read). Several launch-era brands (e.g. Betfred, Crab Sports, SuperBook, ESPN Bet→theScore) have exited or rebranded [unverified this session].

**Licensing framework:** sports wagering was approved by referendum (Nov 2020) and enacted by HB 940 (2021); the Sports Wagering Application Review Commission (SWARC) awards licences and the Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Commission/Agency (MLGCC/MLGCA) qualifies and regulates. Licence classes A-1/A-2 (large venues), B-1/B-2 (small retail) and mobile; up to 60 mobile and 30 Class B licences; 5-year terms. Fee schedule (mobile $500k application; A-1 $2.0m; A-2 $1.0m; B-1 $250k; B-2 $50k; renewal ≈1% of average annual proceeds) is from standing knowledge of HB 940 and marked [unverified this session].

**Fiscal politics point one way:** the 2025 Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act lifted the mobile rate from 15% to 20% (the Governor's opening proposal was 30% [unverified]); Maryland's structural budget gap keeps further increases, or a tightening of promo deductibility, live for the 2027 session.

**Perimeter enforcement is active:** the MLGCA issued cease-and-desist letters to prediction-market platforms (Kalshi, Robinhood, Crypto.com) in April 2025; the resulting KalshiEX v. Martin litigation (preliminary injunction denied at district level, on appeal) remained unresolved as far as could be verified. The regulator maintains a public 'Legal vs. Illegal Online Gaming' page and publishes investigative summaries and decision statements.

**Responsible gambling architecture:** minimum age 21; statewide Voluntary Exclusion Program spanning casinos and sportsbooks; 1-800-GAMBLER and mdgamblinghelp.org funded via the Problem Gambling Fund (expired sports prizes plus casino assessments [unverified]). Advertising rules under COMAR 36.10 restrict under-21 targeting and require RG messaging [detail unverified].

**Payments:** a standard US regulated stack (ACH/online banking, debit, PayPal, prepaid/Play+, cash at retail cages); credit-card funding rules for sports accounts could not be verified this session (n/a). No mobile-money dynamic — payment friction is low and not a differentiator.

**Q4 comparison risk:** Q4 2025 delivered $48.8m of tax (Oct $14.1m, Nov $19.0m — the programme record — Dec $15.7m) on an exceptional hold; Q4 2026 state receipts are likely to be down YoY even with 8–10% handle growth (analyst estimate).

**Read-through for B2Tech:** Maryland is a transparent, moderately taxed (14.7% effective on GGR), fully mobile market with a consolidating mid-tier and no iGaming cross-sell. A greenfield B2C launch faces duopoly customer-acquisition economics in a market where seven challengers share the minority; the realistic entry routes are B2B platform/trading supply to an incumbent or a partnership with a Class A/B venue licence-holder, with the 2027 legislative session (tax, iGaming, prediction markets, sweepstakes) as the key gating event.

segments.name: Mobile sports betting
segments.headline: Volume still compounding (+11.4% Q3) but a 9.9% hold and 2% promo load turned GGR negative and cut state receipts 17.5%.
narrative: Mobile wagering is effectively the whole Maryland sports market: $1,589.1m of the $1,614.5m Q3 handle (98.4%) and $641.2m of September's $652.2m (98.3%). Across the nine months the monthly handle ranged from a trough of $465.9m in August to $652.2m in September, with January ($615.8m) and March ($604.7m) the other two months above $600m. Quarterly stakes ran $1,736.2m in Q1, $1,633.0m in Q2 and $1,614.5m in Q3 — the usual seasonal shape — and the 9M total of $4,983.7m reconciles to the $4.98bn reported by Gaming Intelligence (+9% YoY). The regulator's own fiscal-year table confirms the Q3 comparison: $1,614.5m vs $1,449.3m in Jul–Sep 2025, +11.4%. The caveat is September: +0.2% YoY against a month that already contained the full NFL/college football opening, which is the first flat print in the market's history and warrants monitoring for prediction-market leakage and maturation rather than being written off as calendar noise.

Gross win has not followed. Mobile hold was 11.2% in July, 9.7% in August and 8.8% in September, versus a statewide 11.7% in Q3 2025, so Q3 GGR fell 6.4% to $159.2m and September GGR fell 20.0% to $58.5m (vs $73.1m). The 9M hold of 10.7% (H1 11.1%) remains above the 8–9% seen in older US markets, consistent with Maryland's parlay-heavy mix, so the Q3 shortfall is largely outcome variance plus a tougher comp rather than a structural step-down — but the sport-level split in the regulator's Excel was not read and that judgement is therefore provisional. With H1 GGR of $373.9m and Q3 of $159.2m, calendar 2026 GGR is tracking toward $720–770m (analyst estimate, assuming a 10–11% Q4 hold on $1.9–2.1bn of Q4 stakes), against a 9M run-rate that would otherwise imply ~$710m.

The tax base is 'taxable win': hold less deductible free promotional wagers less 'other amounts'. The arithmetic reconciles cleanly to the federal excise: in September, hold of $58.45m less $10.96m of promo wagers less ~$1.63m (0.25% of $652.2m handle) ≈ $45.9m taxable win as reported. Mobile promo deductions were $11.8m in July (2.4% of mobile handle), $8.9m in August (1.9%) and $10.9m in September (1.7%) — $31.6m for the quarter, 2.0% of stakes — a modest and declining load by US standards and far below any statutory cap, so the deduction is non-binding on operator behaviour. Over 9M, taxable win of $393.1m was 73.7% of GGR, implying $140.1m of deductions, of which an estimated $12.5m was federal excise and ~$127.6m promo (≈2.6% of handle; Jan–Jun split derived from the fund allocation).

Mobile operators paid an estimated $77.3m of the $78.3m 9M state tax (20% of taxable win: 15% to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future education fund and 5% to the General Fund, the latter introduced with the rate rise on 1 July 2025). That equates to 14.7% of GGR — materially lighter than New York (51% of GGR), Pennsylvania (36% with promo deductions) or Illinois (graduated 20–40% plus per-wager levy) and comparable to New Jersey post its 2025 increase [peer benchmarks from standing knowledge, unverified this session]. For an operator, Maryland's economics are therefore better than its 20% headline suggests, but the fiscal trajectory is one-directional: the rate has already moved once and the General Assembly's structural deficit keeps both a further increase and a narrowing of deductions on the table.

Nine mobile brands are reported for September 2026 — bet365, BetMGM, betPARX, BetRivers, Caesars, DraftKings, Fanatics, FanDuel and theScore Bet — down from the launch-era field, with Betfred, Crab Sports, SuperBook and ESPN Bet (replaced by theScore Bet) among the exits or rebrands [unverified this session]. Operator-level handle and GGR shares are n/a here because the regulator's operator spreadsheet could not be read; in comparable eastern US states FanDuel and DraftKings together hold roughly 70–75% of handle and Maryland is understood to follow that pattern [unverified]. The commercial implication for B2Tech is that the contestable pool for a seventh-to-ninth-ranked challenger is in the order of $20–40m of monthly handle, before CAC — thin for a B2C launch, but an addressable B2B opportunity for pricing, trading or platform supply to the mid-tier brands that are visibly under scale pressure.

Outlook for the channel: Q4 2025 produced $48.8m of state tax (Oct $14.1m, Nov $19.0m — a programme record — Dec $15.7m) on an unusually favourable hold, so even with 8–10% handle growth Q4 2026 receipts are likely to be down YoY (analyst view). Calendar 2026 handle is tracking to ~$6.9–7.1bn (estimate) and state tax to ~$105–115m (estimate), versus FY2026's $132.3m which benefited from that windfall.

segments.name: Retail sports betting
segments.headline: A 1.6%-of-handle channel with volatile hold — a brand and compliance footprint, not a P&L.
narrative: Retail sportsbooks handled $25.4m in Q3 2026 (July $7.2m, August $7.1m, September $11.0m) against $1,589.1m mobile, i.e. 1.6% of the market; the share was 1.8% in January ($11.1m of $615.8m). Retail GGR was $3.0m for the quarter on an 11.9% hold, but the monthly hold swung from 8.2% (August) and 8.8% (July) to 16.3% (September), illustrating how thin the base is. Retail taxable win was $2.7m and retail tax $0.41m in Q3 at the 15% rate — roughly 1.7% of total state receipts — and retail promotional wagers are negligible ($15.8k in September, $10.7k in August).

The retail estate comprises the sportsbooks inside the six casinos, stadium and racetrack venues and a tail of Class B off-track-betting and bingo-hall books; the regulator does not publish a venue count in the monthly release and the current number of active retail locations is n/a [standing knowledge suggests mid-teens; unverified]. Retail books in Maryland function as omnichannel acquisition and cash-funding points for the attached mobile brand (MGM/BetMGM, Live!/FanDuel, Horseshoe/Caesars, Northwest Stadium/Fanatics) rather than as standalone profit centres.

For an entrant the retail licence tiers are the cheapest regulated foothold in the state — the Class B-2 application fee is understood to be $50k (B-1 $250k) [per HB 940; unverified this session] — but the revenue opportunity is immaterial: the entire retail channel generated ~$12m of GGR annualised in Q3. A retail-first strategy only makes sense as a brand/compliance anchor for a mobile licence or as a kiosk/self-service B2B play with a venue partner.

Direction of travel is further erosion: retail share has drifted from ~2% at the start of 2026 to 1.6–1.7% in Q3 as mobile growth outpaces a static venue base. There is no legislative momentum to expand retail (e.g. lottery-terminal or bar-top betting), and the Maryland Lottery's own commercial agenda is focused on draw and instant games rather than sports.

segments.name: Land-based casinos & lottery
segments.headline: Six casinos at ~$1.9bn annualised GGR are flat-to-down (Q3 −4%) with no iGaming relief; the Lottery/casino/sports complex still paid a record $1.637bn to the state in FY2026.
narrative: Maryland's six commercial casinos — MGM National Harbor, Live! Casino & Hotel Maryland, Horseshoe Baltimore, Ocean Downs, Hollywood Casino Perryville and Rocky Gap [names from standing knowledge] — generated $151.4m of gaming revenue (VLT plus table games) in September 2026, −0.1% YoY per the regulator's release and secondary coverage, after $160.0m in August and $157.9m in July. The Q3 total of $469.3m was −4% YoY according to Gaming Intelligence, implying July and August were down mid-single digits. The property split, VLT/table mix and 9M calendar total were not read this session and are n/a.

Casino taxation is property-specific: the state's share of VLT revenue varies by licence (historically in a roughly 40–61% band, with Education Trust Fund, local-impact and horse-racing allocations) while table games are taxed at 20% of GGR [rates from standing knowledge; unverified this session]. The MLGCA's 'Where the Money Goes' page is the authoritative allocation reference. Because the casinos carry far heavier effective tax than mobile sportsbooks (14.7% of GGR), the land-based lobby has an obvious interest in both protecting its tax base and shaping any iGaming bill.

Fiscal year 2026 (Jul 2025–Jun 2026) was a record for the state: the Lottery, casinos and sports wagering together contributed $1.637bn (Maryland Lottery release, 7 Aug 2026). Sports wagering supplied $132.3m of that (+48.8% on FY2025's $88.9m); the Lottery and casino components were not separately read and are n/a, but the casinos remain by far the largest contributor. The headline matters politically: the General Assembly has a demonstrated revenue dependency on gaming, which both protects the regulated market's legitimacy and sustains the appetite for higher rates.

iGaming is the swing factor for this segment. A House-passed iGaming bill died in the Senate in 2024 and subsequent attempts have not reached the Governor [status for the 2026 session unverified this session]; casino labour and cannibalisation concerns, plus a constitutional-referendum requirement for new commercial gaming, are the structural obstacles. Until that changes, the land-based estate has no digital growth channel and sportsbooks have no casino cross-sell — a key reason Maryland's online market is smaller per capita than New Jersey, Pennsylvania or Michigan.

For B2Tech, the casino segment is relevant mainly as a partnership route: Class A sports wagering licences sit with these venues and a casino-partnered skin (as Fanatics and bet365 have used elsewhere) remains the conventional market-access model. Any iGaming legalisation would almost certainly tether online casino licences to the six properties, making those relationships the gating asset for any future digital casino play.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: Open multi-licence framework with a GGR-based tax that already moved from 15% to 20% for mobile; next pressure points are the 2027 session and the first 5-year mobile renewals.
narrative: Sports wagering was authorised by constitutional referendum in November 2020 and implemented by HB 940 (2021), codified in the State Government Article (Title 9, Subtitle 1E) with regulations at COMAR 36.10. Retail launched in December 2021 and mobile on 23 November 2022. Two bodies run the regime: the Sports Wagering Application Review Commission (SWARC) awards licences after the Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Commission (MLGCC) completes suitability, and the MLGCA — which also operates the Lottery — regulates day-to-day, publishes monthly operator-level data and issues investigative summaries and decision statements. The framework was explicitly designed to be inclusive (minority and women-owned business participation criteria at SWARC) and numerically open: up to 60 mobile and 30 Class B licences [caps per statute; unverified this session].

Licence classes are venue-driven. Class A-1 (casinos with ≥1,000 VLTs, professional stadiums) and A-2 (smaller casinos, racetracks) carry application fees understood to be $2.0m and $1.0m; Class B-1 and B-2 (small retail venues) $250k and $50k; and a standalone mobile licence $500k, all for five-year terms with renewal fees set at roughly 1% of average annual proceeds [fee schedule from standing knowledge of HB 940; not re-read this session]. The first wave of mobile licences issued in November 2022 therefore comes up for renewal in late 2027 — a natural moment for the regulator to revisit conditions and for sub-scale brands to decide whether to stay.

The tax base is taxable win: gross win less deductible free promotional wagers less 'other amounts', which the monthly arithmetic shows to be the 0.25% federal excise on handle. Retail licensees pay 15% to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund (education). Mobile licensees paid 15% until 30 June 2025 and 20% from 1 July 2025 under the 2025 Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act — 15% to Blueprint and the incremental 5% to the General Fund (the Governor's opening proposal was 30% [unverified]). Expired prizes (unclaimed after 182 days) go to the Problem Gambling Fund. Maryland's statute allows promotional deductions without limit in a licensee's first fiscal year and caps them thereafter (understood to be 20% of handle [unverified]); actual usage is ~2% of mobile handle, so the cap is not a constraint.

Outcomes in 9M 2026: $78.3m of state tax on $533.2m of GGR, an effective 14.7%; $59.0m to Blueprint and $19.3m to the General Fund. The General Fund's cumulative receipt is $38.6m since July 2025, demonstrating the yield from the five-point increase — and, to a legislature facing a structural deficit, the ease of extracting more. The practical risk for operators is less a headline rate jump than the quieter levers: eliminating promo deductibility (worth ~$25m a year of tax base at current intensity), disallowing the federal-excise deduction, or adding a per-wager levy as Illinois has done.

Direction of travel: the 2027 General Assembly session (January–April 2027) is the next decision point for (i) any BRFA tax measure, (ii) an iGaming bill, (iii) a sweepstakes-casino prohibition (a 2025 Senate bill passed one chamber only [unverified]) and (iv) a legislative response to federally-regulated sports event contracts. The regulator's own posture is enforcement-led and transparent; the fiscal posture is extractive. An operator should underwrite Maryland at a 20–25% mobile rate on a narrower base over a three-year horizon.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling, advertising & enforcement
segments.headline: Low-friction US payments, a regulator-run exclusion programme and an active fight over prediction markets and unlicensed online gaming.
narrative: Payments in Maryland follow the standard US regulated stack — ACH/online banking, debit cards, PayPal and similar e-wallets, prepaid Play+ cards, and cash at casino cages and retail books — with mandatory geolocation and identity verification under COMAR 36.10 and a minimum age of 21. Whether credit-card funding of sports wagering accounts is permitted could not be verified this session (n/a); several neighbouring states prohibit it and Maryland bills have proposed similar restrictions [unverified]. There is no mobile-money dimension: payment acceptance is not a competitive differentiator, and the operative constraints are bank-level gambling merchant codes and the operators' own deposit-limit tooling.

Responsible-gambling infrastructure is regulator-centred. The MLGCA administers a statewide Voluntary Exclusion Program covering casinos and sports wagering, and all releases carry the 1-800-GAMBLER helpline and mdgamblinghelp.org (the Maryland Alliance for Responsible Gambling / Center of Excellence on Problem Gambling). Funding runs through the Problem Gambling Fund, which receives expired sports prizes — $5.8m cumulative to September 2026, accreting ~$45–65k a month — plus per-device casino assessments [unverified]. Operators must offer deposit, time and wager limits and self-exclusion tools in-app, and the regulator has issued decision statements on licensee compliance that are published on its website.

Advertising rules under COMAR 36.10 restrict targeting of under-21s and college campuses, require RG messaging and helpline disclosure, and the regulator has moved against misleading promotional language (e.g. 'risk-free') [detail unverified this session]. Maryland also prohibited proposition bets on individual college athletes in 2024 following the NCAA request [unverified]. Relative to Ohio or Massachusetts the advertising regime is moderate; relative to the UK or Italy it is light, with no watershed or sponsorship bans.

Enforcement attention has shifted to the perimeter. In April 2025 the MLGCA sent cease-and-desist letters to Kalshi, Robinhood and Crypto.com over sports event contracts; Kalshi sued (KalshiEX LLC v. Martin), the US District Court for Maryland denied a preliminary injunction and the matter went to the Fourth Circuit [status as of October 2026 unverified]. The regulator maintains a 'Legal vs. Illegal Online Gaming' page and publishes investigative summaries, signalling a willingness to act against offshore and sweepstakes-style operators. September's flat handle makes the leakage question commercially material: every dollar wagered on CFTC-regulated event contracts is outside the 20% state tax and outside Maryland's RG controls.

For B2Tech the implications are twofold. Compliance cost is moderate and predictable (geolocation, KYC, RG tooling, advertising review), and the regulator is transparent and procedurally conventional. The larger uncertainty is regulatory scope: if the courts or Congress entrench federally-regulated sports event contracts, Maryland's licensed operators face an untaxed substitute, and the state's likely response — pressure on payment processors and affiliates, plus legislative definitions — would raise compliance friction for everyone operating in the market.

highlights.text: Volume growth persists in year four: 9M handle $4,983.7m (+9%), Q3 +11.4% YoY — Maryland is still adding stakes faster than most 2021–22 vintage US states.
Moderate effective tax: 14.7% of GGR in 9M 2026 (20% mobile headline on a base net of ~2% promo wagers and federal excise) — far lighter than NY (51%) or PA (36%), supporting operator margins.

Transparent, procedurally stable regulator: monthly operator-level data, published decision statements, an open licence framework (up to 60 mobile licences) with no server-localisation or local-ownership requirements.

Mid-tier consolidation (exits/rebrands of Betfred, Crab Sports, SuperBook, ESPN Bet [unverified]) leaves nine brands and a visible need for pricing/trading/platform efficiency among sub-scale operators — a B2B entry point for B2Tech.

Record FY2026 state contributions ($1.637bn across lottery, casinos and sports; sports $132.3m, +49%) create a strong political constituency for the regulated market and for perimeter enforcement against unlicensed substitutes.
Promo-deduction room: actual promotional wagers run ~2% of handle versus a cap understood to be far higher, so a challenger can fund acquisition tax-efficiently in the launch phase.

lowlights.text: Hold compression: statewide hold fell from 11.7% (Q3 2025) to 9.9% (Q3 2026) and 9.0% in September, turning GGR −6.4%/−20% despite handle growth — partly variance, but the structural hold premium Maryland enjoyed is narrowing.

Fiscal extraction is one-directional: mobile tax rose 15%→20% on 1 Jul 2025 after a 30% proposal [unverified]; a structural budget deficit makes a further rate rise or removal of promo/excise deductibility a live 2027-session risk.

Duopoly economics: FanDuel and DraftKings are understood to control ~70%+ of handle [unverified]; the remaining seven brands share perhaps $20–40m of monthly handle each at best, implying punishing CAC for a B2C newcomer.
No iGaming: repeated legislative failures and a referendum requirement mean no casino cross-sell, capping online ARPU and leaving Maryland smaller per capita than NJ/PA/MI.

Prediction-market leakage: CFTC-regulated sports event contracts are being marketed to Marylanders untaxed; September's flat handle (+0.2%) is the first sign the substitute may be biting, and the KalshiEX v. Martin outcome is unresolved.
Tough Q4 comparison: Q4 2025 generated a record $48.8m of tax on an exceptional hold (Nov $19.0m), so Q4 2026 state receipts and operator GGR are likely to print negative YoY regardless of volume.
Land-based softness: casino GGR −4% in Q3 ($469.3m) raises the odds of the casino lobby seeking relief or shaping any iGaming/tax bill in its favour.

forecast.intro: The reference point is FY2026 (Jul 2025–Jun 2026), when sports wagering returned a record $132.3m to the state, +48.8% on FY2025's $88.9m, as the mobile rate stepped from 15% to 20% and the Q4 2025 hold windfall ($48.8m in Oct–Dec) landed. FY2027 has opened at $24.6m for Q1 (−17.5%): the rate uplift has fully annualised, hold normalised from 11.7% to 9.9% and promo deductions remain ~2% of handle. Our bridge from FY2026 to FY2027 is therefore handle growth (+) more than offset by hold normalisation and the loss of the Q4 windfall (−), with no rate change assumed until any 2027-session measure takes effect from 1 July 2027.
forecast.view: **Market:** calendar-2026 handle should land at ~$6.9–7.1bn (estimate) and GGR at ~$720–770m (estimate), with hold reverting toward 10–11% rather than the 11–12% of 2024–25 as parlay pricing competition and prediction-market substitution erode the structural premium. Handle growth decelerates to mid-single digits in 2027 absent new product (iGaming) — September's +0.2% is the early warning. **Margins:** operator economics remain among the better in the US north-east at a ~15% effective GGR tax, but we would underwrite a 20–25% mobile rate on a narrower base (promo and/or excise deductions removed) within two sessions; the fiscal signal is unambiguous. **Structure:** expect further mid-tier attrition toward 6–8 mobile brands by the late-2027 renewal window, with B2B supply and casino-partnered skins the realistic entry routes. **Regulatory direction:** enforcement-led perimeter defence (prediction markets, sweepstakes) is more likely than product liberalisation; iGaming remains a <50% probability for 2027 given the referendum requirement and casino/labour opposition.
